lines: Finding five surprised me. Almost nobody uses these tools as published.

Two interviewees used a tool on its defaults. Everyone else extended a tool with their own skills and workflow layers, or built their own. On Reddit, building your own SDD tool was the single most frequent code.
So the tool is a starter kit more than a product.
That's how practitioners treat it. And the most common shape in public repos is the change-scoped spec. The median repo holds nineteen specs, with a median length of about six hundred seventy words.
Let's do benefits. What do people actually get?
The most widely reported benefit is more reliable agent work. Better code, less rework, and longer tasks with less babysitting. Eighteen of the twenty-one interviewees described it.

[thoughtful] But nobody could separate that from the models simply getting better over the same period. One participant concluded it's largely the models. And on Reddit, one team ran SDD for months and said they couldn't prove it improved the code.
What about collaboration? That's the enterprise pitch.

It showed up only where specs actually passed between developers and other roles. A product owner saying, now I see what my developers are doing. In developer-only teams, the benefit was modest. And tool makers mostly described collaboration as a purpose of specs, not something they had observed.
And the third benefit is subtler.

Clarifying intent. The agent asks questions and drafts a spec, and reading the draft shows you what it understood and what you haven't decided yet. As one tool maker put it, authoring a spec clarifies the objective, even to yourself.
